knownFor: Death of Øystein I of Norway on 29 August 1123
A royal estate first recorded at the moment of that death
The end of the twenty-year joint reign with Sigurd the Crusader
One of several Norwegian farms called Hustad, so the identification rests on tradition
overview: A Norwegian royal estate on the Romsdal coast associated with Øystein I’s death in 1123.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Hustad in Møre og Romsdal on the Norwegian coast was where Øystein I of Norway died in 1123, before his co-ruling brother Sigurd the Crusader. His death ended the cooperative joint reign that had characterized Norwegian kingship during the brothers’ shared rule.

The place was a kongsgård, a royal farm: one of the estates the crown held directly up and down the coast, where a travelling king and his household could be fed and housed. Norwegian kingship in this period had no capital and worked by moving between such places, so dying at one of them was the ordinary way for a king to die.

contentSections.title: Which Hustad
paragraphs: Hustad is not a rare name. It means, plainly, the house-stead, and farms of the name are scattered across Norway. The sagas record only that Øystein died at Hustad, without naming a district, so the identification of the place is a matter of which Hustad the later record supports.

The tradition attaches to the royal estate in Romsdal, on the exposed coast of what is now Hustadvika municipality: it is documented as a kongsgård, it remained a noble seat for centuries afterwards — passing to the Rosenkrantz family in the sixteenth century and later to the Urne and Frimann families — and its earliest notice in the record is precisely the king’s death there in 1122 or 1123. The confusion that does arise is with Hustad in Inderøy, in Trøndelag, a medieval chieftain’s seat beside its own medieval church, which produced an archbishop of Nidaros in the thirteenth century. The Romsdal estate is the one the tradition names; the Trøndelag farm is the one it is most often mistaken for.

contentSections.title: The death of Øystein, 1123
paragraphs: By the saga accounts the king was taken ill at a feast at Hustad and died there on 29 August 1123, in his mid-thirties. His body was carried to Nidaros and buried in the cathedral church.

Snorri Sturluson wrote that no man’s grave in Norway was ever stood over by so many mourners as Øystein’s. That is a saga writer’s judgement a century later rather than a count, but it fits the reputation the same sources give him, and it is the closest thing to an epitaph the place has.

contentSections.title: The king who stayed at home
paragraphs: Øystein I is remembered for domestic building projects — roads, harbors, and churches — during his reign alongside Sigurd, contrasting with Sigurd’s crusading campaigns. The saga tradition sets the two brothers against each other deliberately, and even stages a formal contest of boasting between them.

The works credited to Øystein are specific enough to be checked against the landscape: the church and the fishermen’s booths at Vågan in Lofoten, the harbour at Agdenes at the mouth of the Trondheimsfjord, shelters for travellers crossing the Dovre mountains at Hjerkinn, the royal hall and Munkeliv abbey at Bergen, and dry docks at Nidaros. They are the acts of a king investing in the coast his ships and his fishermen used.

contentSections.title: After the joint reign
paragraphs: His death at Hustad left Sigurd as sole ruler and set the conditions for the succession instability that followed Sigurd’s own death in 1130. The joint rule of the brothers from 1103 had lasted twenty years, the longest in Norwegian history, and it had worked.

What came after it did not. The civil wars that opened in 1130 ran, with intervals, for more than a century, and the orderly sharing of a kingdom between brothers that Øystein and Sigurd managed was never repeated. Nothing of the royal estate survives above ground today.

name: Hustad
summary: The royal estate on the Romsdal coast where Øystein I died in 1123, ending the longest joint reign in Norwegian history — one of several farms of the name, and identified by tradition rather than by the sagas.
